extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of advanced undergraduate/graduate real analysis (metric spaces)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts definitions, hypotheses, and theorem-conditions about metric-space topics (Baire Category, Ascoli, Stone–Weierstrass, completion, C(S) compactness) from a real-analysis textbook chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nowhere dense / open dense
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed set in a metric space is nowhere dense if its interior is empty. Its complement is an open dense set, and conversely the complement of any open dense set is closed nowhere dense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor set as closed nowhere dense example
rubrics_metrics.description: A Cantor set in R constructed by iteratively removing middle open intervals (fractions r1, r2, ...) is closed (intersection of closed sets) and nowhere dense because it contains no interval of more than one point. For the standard Cantor set start with [0,1] and remove middle thirds (r1 = r2 = ... = 1/3). The 'length' (Lebesgue measure) of the resulting set equals the product of the complementary fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a nontrivial example of a closed nowhere dense set; can be inserted repeatedly into removed intervals to produce dense unions of closed nowhere dense sets (see examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Baire Category Theorem (Theorem 2.53)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,d) is a complete metric space, then (a) the intersection of countably many open dense sets is nonempty, and (b) X is not the union of countably many closed nowhere dense sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are equivalent by taking complements. Remark: in (a) the intersection is actually dense, not merely nonempty; no nonempty open subset of X can be contained in a countable union of closed nowhere dense sets. Proof uses an inductive construction of nested balls and completeness (Cauchy sequences converge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationals not a countable intersection of open sets (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subset Q of rationals in R is not the countable intersection of open sets: if Q = ∩_{n=1}^∞ U_n with U_n open then each U_n is dense, so ∩ U_n would be dense (by Baire) and nonempty, contradicting Q being meagre in R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates application of Baire Category Theorem to classical sets; used to show certain descriptive set-theoretic statements fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: First category (meagre) set
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset E of a metric space is of the first category if it is contained in the countable union of closed nowhere dense sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 2.53 implies that in a complete metric space no nonempty open set is of the first category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscillation of a function and Lemma 2.55
rubrics_metrics.description: Define osc_g(x0) = lim_{δ→0} sup_{y ∈ B(δ;x0)} |g(y) - g(x0)|. Lemma 2.55: for a metric space (U,d) and g:U→C, and any ε>0, the set {x : osc_g(x) ≥ ε} is contained in the closure of {x : osc_g(x) > ε/2} and conversely inclusion bounds show these oscillation-level sets relate by closure and constant factors (explicitly the lemma gives inclusions showing certain level sets are relatively closed and bounded by factors of 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to control discontinuity sets: the oscillation detects continuity (osc=0 iff continuous) and to show appropriate sets are closed/relatively closed in proofs such as Theorem 2.54.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuity set of pointwise limit (Theorem 2.54)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (X,d) be a complete metric space and U an open subset. Suppose fn:U→C are continuous and fn → f pointwise on U. Then the set of discontinuities of f is of the first category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: use the oscillation notion and Lemma 2.55 to show level sets of oscillation do not contain nonempty open subsets; apply Baire Category Theorem to conclude the discontinuity set is meagre. Construction uses closed sets A_{m,n} and the fact that some A_m has nonempty interior would contradict continuity of approximants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equicontinuous / pointwise bounded / uniformly equicontinuous / uniformly bounded (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F be a set of scalar-valued functions on compact metric space S. F is equicontinuous at x if for each ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that d(t,x) < δ implies |f(t)-f(x)| < ε for all f ∈ F. F is pointwise bounded if for each t ∈ S there exists M_t with |f(t)| ≤ M_t for all f ∈ F. F is uniformly equicontinuous on S if δ can be chosen independent of x. F is uniformly bounded on S if a single M works for all t ∈ S and all f ∈ F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the hypotheses for Ascoli's theorem and for the characterization of relatively compact subsets of C(S) when S is compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascoli's Theorem (Theorem 2.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (S,d) be a compact metric space. If {f_n} is a sequence of scalar-valued functions on S that is equicontinuous at each point of S and pointwise bounded on S, then (a) {f_n} is uniformly equicontinuous and uniformly bounded on S, and (b) {f_n} has a uniformly convergent subsequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: range R or C may be replaced by any compact metric space. Proof uses compactness (Bolzano–Weierstrass), a countable dense set D in S, and Cantor diagonal process to extract a subsequence convergent on D then extend uniform Cauchy control via equicontinuity to all of S. Part (a) shows that pointwise equicontinuity + pointwise boundedness actually imply uniform versions on compact S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of compact subsets of C(S) (Corollary 2.57)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (S,d) is a compact metric space, then a subset E of C(S) (with the uniform metric) has compact closure if and only if E is uniformly bounded and uniformly equicontinuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: uniform limits preserve these properties so closure inherits them; conversely if E is closed, uniformly bounded and equicontinuous, Ascoli shows every sequence in E has a subsequence convergent in C(S), hence E is compact. Uses total boundedness and compactness of C(S) criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subalgebra and separation of points (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subalgebra of C(S,R) or C(S,C) is a nonempty subset closed under pointwise addition, scalar multiplication and pointwise multiplication (and for complex case, closure under complex conjugation is considered). A subalgebra separates points if for each pair of distinct points x1, x2 in S there exists f in the subalgebra with f(x1) ≠ f(x2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closure of a subalgebra in the uniform metric is again a subalgebra; in the complex case closure under conjugation is required in Stone–Weierstrass (part (b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stone–Weierstrass Theorem (Theorem 2.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If A is a subalgebra of C(S,R) that separates points and contains the constant functions, then Ā (closure of A) is dense in C(S,R) in the uniform metric. (b) If A is a subalgebra of C(S,C) that separates points, contains the constant functions, and is closed under complex conjugation, then Ā is dense in C(S,C) in the uniform metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline (real case): use closure under max/min, construct for each x a gx ∈ Ā that is close to f at x and uniformly larger elsewhere, extract finitely many via compactness to produce h ∈ Ā with h(s) > f(s) - ε, then combine to approximate f. For complex case reduce to real and imaginary parts and apply (a). Examples and counterexamples illustrate necessity of hypotheses (e.g., need conjugation for complex-valued algebra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: separability of C(S) (Corollary 2.59)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (S,d) is a compact metric space, then C(S) is separable as a metric space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a countable base of S and for pairs (U,V) with Ū ⊆ V define continuous functions f_{U,V} separating points; finite products and rational linear combinations yield a countable algebra D whose closure (by Stone–Weierstrass) is C(S,C), so D is dense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isometry (definition) and completion existence (Theorem 2.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: An isometry of X into Y is a map φ:X→Y preserving distances: ρ(φ(x1),φ(x2)) = d(x1,x2) for all x1,x2 ∈ X. Theorem 2.60: For any metric space (X,d) there exists a complete metric space (X*,ρ) and an isometry φ:X→X* whose image is dense in X*. (X*,ρ) is called a completion of (X,d) and is essentially unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction by equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences in X: define relation p_n ∼ q_n iff lim_n d(p_n,q_n)=0; set X* = set of equivalence classes and define ρ(P,Q)=lim_n d(p_n,q_n). Show this is well-defined, metric, complete; embed X via constant sequences. This standard construction yields the completion; uniqueness up to isometry is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: connected but not pathwise connected set (illustration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction: the closure of a certain graph together with all points (0,t) for t in [something] is connected by Proposition 2.52, but this closure is not pathwise connected; hence this is an example of a connected set in R^2 that is not pathwise connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used earlier in the chapter to distinguish connectedness and pathwise-connectedness; shows pathwise-connected implies connected but not conversely.
